newsitem.title: USA: Group urges NYS pay for what it requires of cities.
newsitem.headline: Group urges NYS pay for what it requires of cities.

text.p: Civic and local groups, seeking to reduce the pressure on property taxes, on Friday urged New York state to pay more for costly programs that it imposes on counties, cities and towns, especially Medicaid.

Noting that most states do not require counties to pay part of the costs of Medicaid, Dave Lucas, a spokesman for the New York Association of Counties, said that the state's 58 counties now spend around $3.8 billion a year for the plan.
"That's all paid for with property taxes," said Lucas.

Another program that the counties have little control over but must contribute to is pre-schooling for special students. The counties' share of this program amounts to $350 million, about 40.5 percent of its cost. "It's the next Medicaid," Lucas said, noting the program's costs have risen sharply.
County officials argued that by forcing them to pay for such programs, the legislature was increasing the pressure to raise local property taxes.

"Local officials find themselves regularly faced with the Hobson's choice of cutting back on other locally-sponsored public benefit programs and services or raising local property taxes," said Grant Bishop, of Erie County, in prepared remarks.

The association of counties was joined by municipal groups and the New York Farm Bureau, as well as state Senator Michael Hoblock, R-Albany County, and Assemblywoman Sandra Galef, R-Westchester county, at a news conference.
Lucas added that the Business Council of New York, which also supports legislation the two state elected officials have proposed to combat the problem, could not attend as it was holding a retreat.

The proposed bill would require New York to appropriate funds to compensate counties for new mandates that cost one locality $10,000 impact or $100,000 collectively. While the legislature still could enact unfunded mandates, a three-fifths vote would be required.

However, one thorn in the side of the county association was removed, as Gov. George Pataki recently signed a bill, which was part of the budget, which releases almost $200 million of payments for the counties for pre-school programs.

"We're hoping that around $198 million will be released," said Patricia Snieska, deputy executive director of the New York County Association. Once the funds are released, the county has agreed to dismiss without prejudice a suit it had filed to force the state to pay for the claims.
Still, even when this money is paid, the state will owe the counties another $150 million, Lucas said, noting that paperwork delays can hold up claims for as long as three years.
